address.definition: A public code that identifies a wallet. Others need it to send you coins.

wallet.definition: An app or device that holds the keys to your coins and lets you send and receive them.

private-key.definition: A secret code that proves you own the coins at an address. Whoever has it can move them.

seed-phrase.definition: 12 or 24 words that can restore a wallet and all its keys. Never share it with anyone.

transaction.definition: A transfer of coins from one address to another, recorded on the blockchain.

fee.definition: A small payment to the network for processing a transaction.

irreversible.definition: Cannot be undone. A confirmed crypto transaction cannot be cancelled or refunded.

blockchain.definition: A shared record of transactions, kept by many computers, that cannot be changed quietly.

airdrop.definition: A free handout of coins or tokens to many wallets. Real ones exist, but fake airdrops are a common trick to make you connect your wallet.

phishing.definition: A trick where scammers pretend to be someone you trust, often with a fake message or website, to steal your passwords or seed phrase.

cryptocurrency.definition: Digital money that runs on a network of computers instead of a bank. Bitcoin was the first.

block.definition: A batch of transactions added to a blockchain together. Each block is linked to the one before it.

exchange.definition: A platform where people buy and sell cryptocurrencies, often for euros or dollars. Most are for adults only.

volatility.definition: How much and how fast a price goes up and down. Crypto prices are very volatile.

rug-pull.definition: A scam where the creators of a coin collect buyers' money and then disappear, leaving the coin almost worthless.

kyc.definition: Short for "know your customer": the identity check a licensed platform does before you can use it, usually with an ID document.

token.definition: A coin created on top of an existing blockchain instead of having its own. Anyone can create one in minutes.

stablecoin.definition: A coin that tries to stay worth the same as normal money, such as 1 euro or 1 dollar.

confirmation.definition: Each new block added after the one with your transaction. More confirmations make it harder to change.

two-factor.definition: A second step when logging in, such as a code from an app, as well as your password.

leverage.definition: Trading with borrowed money. It makes both wins and losses many times bigger.
